item.title: Towards an Operational Proof-theoretic Semantics
item.description: arXiv:2611.00030v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Model-theoretic semantics comes with a computational counterpart: to check validity is to search for a countermodel, and tableaux, resolution, and satisfiability solvers make the semantics something one can run. Proof-theoretic semantics -- the younger paradigm in which meaning is given by inferential role rather than by denotation -- has no established counterpart. This paper proposes one: logic programming. We show that Sandqvist's base-extension semantics for intuitionistic propositional logic is executable in a precise sense. Bases are logic programs, and to each formula $\varphi$ we assign a goal $[\![\varphi]\!]$ of a second-order hereditary Harrop language such that $\varphi$ is supported in a base $\mathcal{B}$ exactly when $[\![\varphi]\!]$ is operationally derivable from $\mathcal{B}$ read as a program. The encoding is the Russell-Prawitz translation of the connectives with quantification restricted to atoms, and this restriction is not a limitation but the point: it is what the support clauses themselves demand. The correspondence is exact base by base, not merely at the level of validity, so that intuitionistic validity becomes the success of a single query against the empty program. Logic programming stands to proof-theoretic semantics as tableaux and satisfiability solvers stand to model-theoretic semantics.
item.dc:creator: Alexander V. Gheorghiu

item.title: Univalent Non-Associative Categorical Structures
item.description: arXiv:2611.00068v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study category-like structures in which composition is not associative, especially Munch-Maccagnoni's duploids, in univalent foundations. Included is a definition of what a univalent duploid is: one where isomorphisms of a suitable kind render the objects indistinguishable to the type theory. We show that the existing construction of a duploid from an adjunction is not univalent as a "single-sorted" duploid, and provide a novel construction which is. This work is formalized in the UniMath library for the Rocq proof assistant.
item.dc:creator: Beatrice Szilvasy

item.title: Blazing-Fast SMT-LIB Parsing for Rust and Lean
item.description: arXiv:2611.00185v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: SMT-LIB is a standard input format for Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) solvers. However, parsing the format is non-trivial and can become a bottleneck, e.g. when retrieving benchmark metadata or normalising the input for solvers. We introduce blazing-smtlib, a Rust parsing library for SMT-LIB, and BSmtLib, its port to Lean. We outline the library API we designed for composability and extensibility (including non-standard SMT-LIB commands), and discuss our implementation decisions for fast lexing and parsing. We proved that our lexing and parsing with Lean-specific optimisations match our formalised reading of the SMT-LIB syntax. We measured performance on a representative sample from the 2025 SMT-LIB corpus and found that blazing-smtlib is more than 6 times faster on the geometric mean than previous parsing libraries and BSmtLib is faster or comparable to them.
item.dc:creator: Jan Onderka, Armin Biere, Henrik B\"oving

item.title: A polynomial-size logical twin for neural networks
item.description: arXiv:2611.01146v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A logical twin of a neural network is a logical representation that mimics the computation of the network through logical formulas. We revisit two earlier proposals for constructing logical twins of feedforward neural networks in {\L}ukasiewicz logic, both of which are susceptible to exponential blow-up in running time and representation size. Building on ideas from both approaches, we present a new construction that directly yields logical twins in {\L}ukasiewicz logic. We show that this construction can be computed in polynomial time and produces polynomial-size logical twins. Finally, we report an empirical evaluation of the three methods, showing that the new proposal substantially outperforms the other two.
item.dc:creator: Sandro Preto, Marcelo Finger

item.title: ProofPatch: Reviewing Lean Statements and Keeping the Reviews Valid as Formalizations Evolve
item.description: arXiv:2611.01357v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The kernel of the Lean proof assistant checks that a proof establishes its statement. Whether the statement says what was intended is left to human reviewers. This is the old problem of validating a specification, and it grows more pressing as language models write formal statements in bulk and agents edit formal developments continuously. We present ProofPatch, a tool that helps reviewers judge Lean statements and keeps their judgments valid while the development changes. A reviewer can ask the kernel targeted questions about a statement, such as whether a hypothesis is needed or whether a counterexample exists. Each decision is stored with fingerprints of the statement as Lean elaborated it and of the definitions it depends on, and any declaration can be pinned so that a patch changing it is blocked, whether a person or an agent built on a large language model (LLM) wrote the patch. Working on elaborated terms rather than source text is the central design choice: notation and formatting changes leave a decision intact, and a changed definition reaches every theorem that uses it. On 229 pairs of consecutive revisions of Mathlib, Lean's mathematics library, ProofPatch sends 118 of 12,898 synthetic decisions back for review. Every text-based alternative misses at least 38 of these or sends back at least 13 times as many. On 1,527 labeled statements, kernel evidence flags unfaithful ones with precision 0.88 to 0.96, and in 344 runs of an LLM agent no change to a pinned statement got through.
item.dc:creator: Xujun Che, Depeng Xu, Jian Xiang, Taufiqua Khan

item.title: Computons for Control-Driven Boolean Circuits
item.description: arXiv:2611.01837v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Boolean circuits abstract away from physical implementation details to capture the logical structure and computational behaviour of digital components. Despite their long history of study, their compositional foundations have received comparatively little attention. Building on the theoretical foundations of computons introduced in previous work, we develop a concrete and operationally defined model of computation for control-driven Boolean circuits. We introduce colimit-based operators for composing circuits into sequential, parallel, branching and iterative structures, supported by concrete operational semantics grounded in particular abstract computing devices. The framework refines the semantics of composition, establishes the algebraic properties of its operators and introduces atomic circuits to support more expressive computation units. We demonstrate the applicability of the proposed framework through examples from propositional logic, biomedicine and electronics, and establish an operational equivalence with respect to classical Boolean circuits through a systematic transformation that accommodates gates of arbitrary arity. By this equivalence, we show that control-driven Boolean circuits are at least as powerful as their classical counterpart. That is, they are capable of non-uniformly computing any Boolean function over inputs of arbitrary length. Implementations in Idris and Java demonstrate the practical realisability of the framework.
item.dc:creator: Damian Arellanes

item.title: Homomorphisms on a product of free convex semilattices
item.description: arXiv:2611.02142v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Convex semilattices form an equational class that combines convex algebras and semilattices by a distributive law. For a set $I$ let $\mathcal FI$ be the free convex semilattice with basis $I$. A product $\mathcal FI\times\mathcal FJ$ is generated by $I\times J$, but is not free. Hence, not every map from $I\times J$ into an arbitrary convex semilattice $X$ extends uniquely to a homomorphism from $\mathcal FI\times\mathcal FJ$ to $X$. We investigate a condition on a map $\varphi$ of $I\times J$ into some convex semilattice $X$ that is always necessary and often sufficient for $\varphi$ to have such an extension to a homomorphism $\Phi$ of $\mathcal FI\times\mathcal FJ$ into $X$.
item.dc:creator: Ana Sokolova, Harald Woracek

item.title: Math Foundation Formalization Agent: A General-Purpose Approach to Formalizing Mathematical Foundations
item.description: arXiv:2611.02843v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mathematical formalization plays an important role in establishing rigorous and machine-verifiable foundations for mathematical reasoning. With the development of large language models (LLMs) and interactive theorem provers, intelligent agents offer a promising approach to automating the formalization of mathematical theories. This paper presents the Math Foundation Formalization Agent (MFF-Agent), a general-purpose intelligent agent designed to support formalization tasks across multiple mathematical domains. The agent integrates the reasoning capabilities of large language models with the formal verification capabilities of the Rocq proof assistant. It incorporates task classification, tool-assisted execution, verification feedback, and state-based task management to support the generation, refinement, and verification of formal proofs. Unlike an approach focused on a single mathematical theory, the agent is examined through case studies involving Morse--Kelley axiomatic set theory (MK), real numbers, propositional logic, and equivalences of the axiom of choice. These cases investigate its applicability across mathematical foundations and distinguish source-level completion, interactive verification, and reproducible compilation. The results demonstrate the feasibility of a unified operational framework for heterogeneous foundation-level tasks and clarify the gap between such a framework and a fully integrated mathematical foundation.
item.dc:creator: Jiaxin Xie, Guowei Dou, Xiang Ji, Wensheng Yu

item.title: Propositional Dynamic Logic with Program Costs
item.description: arXiv:2611.02971v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce $\mathbb{N}\mathtt{PDL}$, a resource-aware variant of Propositional Dynamic Logic ($\mathtt{PDL}$) capable of accounting for program costs measured by natural numbers (such as time or space in the sense of computability theory). In this framework, programs correspond to transition systems weighted by extended natural numbers, and the syntax of our logic includes formulas expressing which properties are reachable by program executions within specific cost constraints. First, we explain how the standard program constructs of non-deterministic choice, sequential composition, iteration, and tests are interpreted in this weighted setting and establish the validity of their corresponding reduction axioms. Using an appropriate adaptation of the (Fischer-Ladner) filtration technique, we proceed to prove decidability and completeness for $\mathbb{N}\mathtt{PDL}$ as our main results. We furthermore provide upper and lower complexity bounds for this logic using translations between standard $\mathtt{PDL}$ and $\mathbb{N}\mathtt{PDL}$.
item.dc:creator: Krishna Manoorkar, Wolfgang Poiger

item.title: Final coalgebras over R-modules
item.description: arXiv:2611.03174v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Final coalgebras and the coinduction principle for coalgebras over $R$-modules, where $R$ is a commutative ring, are essential in determining the denotational behaviour of various types of linear weighted automata. The goal of this paper is to provide lower and upper bounds on the ordinals that are needed to construct final coalgebras over $R$-modules as the limit of a transfinite sequence of functor iterations. We give an example of a binary intersection preserving finitary functor on the category of abelian groups, which is the category of modules over integers, that fails to converge in $\omega \cdot 2$ steps, thus settling an open problem of Ad\'{a}mek, Milius, and Moss. Then we relate this to the failure of the Artinian property of the integers and show that all finitary functors on $R$-modules for a Noetherian ring $R$ with Krull dimension $n$, which preserve countable directed intersections and a generalised notion of monomorphism, converge in $\omega \cdot (n + 2)$ steps. We also establish how the connection between Aczel-Mendler bisimulation and behavioural equivalence is mediated by the functor $\operatorname{Ext}^1$. These results show that homological algebra tools can play an important role in coalgebra.
item.dc:creator: Ois\'{i}n Flynn-Connolly, Henning Basold, Chase Ford

item.title: On Small Universal Reversible Turing Machines
item.description: arXiv:2611.00153v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A reversible Turing machine (RTM) is a Turing machine in which every instantaneous description has at most one predecessor. Writing URTM(m,n) for a universal RTM with m states and n symbols, we construct URTM(3,600), URTM(4,41), URTM(5,37), URTM(6,30), URTM(7,28), URTM(8,21), and URTM(85,2); each of them has fewer states or fewer symbols than each of the nine URTMs in Morita's book (2017). They come from improved versions of Morita's conversions to three states, to four states, and to two symbols; for example, the improved conversion to three states uses O(mn^2) symbols instead of O(m^2n^3). We also show that the halting problem of RTMs with at most two states is decidable for finite instantaneous descriptions, so that no RTM with at most two states is universal under any notion of universality that reduces the halting problem of Turing machines to it by a computable encoding into finite instantaneous descriptions; in particular, there is no URTM with at most two states in our formalization of Morita's definition. We also show that no three-state, two-symbol RTM is universal in that formalization.
item.dc:creator: T. Yokoyama

item.title: Coinduction in Grounded Arithmetic
item.description: arXiv:2611.00176v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A grounded arithmetic counts a sentence as true only when a terminating process establishes it; a sentence no such process settles has no value. Such a logic can state that an event happens, but not that it never happens under unbounded choice. This paper extends such a logic so that it can. The base is Reflective Grounded Arithmetic (RGA) with Inductive Grounded Arithmetic (IGA)'s least-fixed-point reading and ground induction. It adds a separate greatest-fixed-point former $\nu$ with Park's coinduction rule, proves that one former cannot carry both ground induction and coinduction, and adds a dichotomy rule: the classical disjunction between a least-fixed-point atom and the greatest-fixed-point atom of its dual, under a derivable premise that the body's leaves are decided. The systems are sound for an explicit model reading every $\nu$-body at its greatest fixed point, hence consistent; they agree with the least model wherever it has a value and prove sentences it leaves without one. The dichotomy replaces the underivable hypothesis that an order is well-founded by the derivable one that its steps are decided; the change of model pays for the move. With ground induction the dichotomy derives the omniscience rule of the sibling arithmetic OGA, so the system has no semantics whose certificates for universals are its own proofs. The systems prove, as single sentences, that every decided tree is well-founded or has an infinite branch given by a term, total in the new model; that random assignment terminates while its divergent twin runs forever; that a fair loop terminates and the alternating-bit protocol delivers every message; that open games are determined; that the termination gap in Nakata and Uustalu's trace semantics closes; and that Cinderella wins the bucket game at capacity three. Isabelle/HOL checks every result.
item.dc:creator: Bryan Ford

item.title: VerusWeave: A Benchmark for Proof Repair in Concurrent Verus Programs
item.description: arXiv:2611.00287v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Concurrent software underpins critical infrastructure, including operating systems and databases, yet thread interactions can have bugs that bypass conventional testing. Verus extends Rust with formal verification capabilities, enabling developers to specify, implement and prove the correctness of concurrent code in the same language. Although coding agents have been explored for automated proof construction, existing Verus benchmarks offer limited coverage of concurrency-specific examples that connect atomic operations to abstract protocols. To address this gap, we introduce VerusWeave, the first benchmark dedicated to concurrent proof repair, derived from four open-source projects. It comprises 75 focused tasks and 17 full-module variants that exercise features used to verify low-level concurrent code. Tasks remove selected proof annotations and require agents to fill gaps, while preserving executable code and specifications. The evaluation harness validates repairs using Verus and a change checker, recording solutions, execution traces, and resource usage. An initial evaluation of four general-purpose coding-agent harnesses achieved 75-85% success on focused tasks and 29-47% on full-module variants, highlighting the challenge of autonomous module-wide repairs. VerusWeave provides a reusable foundation for evaluating automated proof construction for concurrent software.
item.dc:creator: Pedro Ribeiro, Martim Afonso, Andr\'e Vasconcelos, Jo\~ao F. Ferreira

item.title: Order-Invariant CFO Contains Local-Order-Invariant FO
item.description: arXiv:2611.01501v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Order-invariant cluster first-order logic (CFO) and local-order-invariant first-order logic are two fragments of order-invariant first-order logic, both motivated by the study of invariant logics on classes of bounded degree. Our main result is that order-invariant CFO contains local-order-invariant FO on arbitrary classes of finite structures, settling the conjecture of Ghasemi and Grange that order-invariant CFO contains plain FO. By combining this with a collapse result of Ghasemi and Grange, we obtain the equivalence of FO, local-order-invariant FO, and order-invariant CFO on classes of finite colored graphs of bounded degree. The proof makes use of Gaifman normal form, which allows our translation from local-order-invariant FO to order-invariant CFO to be effective. Combined with the fixed-parameter tractability of model-checking for order-invariant CFO on bounded-degree colored graph classes, this shows that model-checking for local-order-invariant FO on bounded-degree colored graph classes is fixed-parameter tractable. To generalize our collapse and model-checking results beyond colored graphs, we use a method based on first-order interpretations which also yields a collapse of order-invariant FO to FO when restricted to graph classes of bounded shrub-depth. Finally, we give an application to the database-motivated frozen-witness logic of Abiteboul, Simon, and Vianu by showing that local-order-invariant FO contains deterministic frozen-witness FO, and thus that deterministic frozen-witness FO collapses to FO on classes of finite structures of bounded degree.
item.dc:creator: Derek R. Aoki

item.title: The Scope Grammar of Natural-Language Rules: Counting and Enumerating Readings modulo Logical Equivalence
item.description: arXiv:2611.01825v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A rule written for people fixes its atomic conditions and connectives but leaves open how the connectives are bracketed, and each bracketing is a different logical reading that an autoformalizer must resolve or expose. We study the scope grammar, a deliberately ambiguous context-free grammar whose derivation trees are the readings of a connective skeleton and whose quotient by logical equivalence is what matters downstream. A skeleton with $k$ binary connectives has $C_k$ derivation trees, the $k$-th Catalan number, but far fewer logically distinct readings. For the positive, repetition-free fragment we make the gap exact: through the uniqueness of the read-once normal form we characterize the realizable normal forms by lowest common ancestors and count them with a two-label recurrence over the operator word, verified against exhaustive enumeration up to eleven atoms. The count is invariant under reversal and $\wedge/\vee$ duality; a skeleton is ambiguous if and only if it uses both $\wedge$ and $\vee$, a one-pass test; and the number of classes is at least $2^{\lfloor n/3\rfloor}$. Up to fifteen atoms the alternating pattern is the worst case; its count has a cubic generating function, is the 3-Schr\"oder sequence (OEIS A137842), and grows with base $\varphi^{5/2}\approx3.330$, below the Catalan base 4. We reduce maximality to an inequality on increments, verified to sixteen atoms, and explain why local exchange arguments cannot prove it. We also treat negation, exceptions, and background axioms, where normal-form uniqueness still decides equivalence but counting is open.
item.dc:creator: Sherzod Turaev, Mary John

item.title: Modern Software Engineering with Verification Agents: A Spec-First Architecture for Autonomous Synthesis, Verification IRs, and Organizational Scale
item.description: arXiv:2611.02285v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: When autonomous coding agents synthesize implementation code, formal specifications, and mechanical proofs simultaneously, the software engineering hierarchy inverts: the formal specification becomes the primary human-reviewed artifact, while source code and proof scripts become disposable build outputs. This paper presents an end-to-end architecture for agent-authored, formally verified software engineering. First, we establish a logic-agnostic foundation combining a spec-first stack inversion, a zero-code-review workflow gated by automated continuous integration (CI) checks, and a minimal Verification Intermediate Representation (VIR) lowered via a thin, verified translator. Second, we pair an extensional Computational Type Theory (CTT) specification layer with Higher-Order Abstract Syntax (HOAS) and linear resource typing in the VIR--eliminating rewrite friction for synthesis agents while defining an experiment, its protocol frozen before the first reader, to measure whether removing boundary coercions improves human specification readability. Third, we scale collaboration across multi-team organizations using Personal Spec-Copilots and a Shared Synthesis Fleet that detects cross-team Semantic Merge Conflicts and fuses modular contracts into zero-copy binaries. We illustrate this architecture on a zero-copy authenticated message router and distinguish our existing empirical baselines (salt, SaltBench, x86lean, and MetaPRL) from newly proposed components.
item.dc:creator: Jason Hickey

item.title: Iterated Narrow Networks: Turing Completeness at Width 4 on Convex Input Spaces and the Complexity of Verification
item.description: arXiv:2611.02840v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the iterates of a fixed ReLU network $N$ of width 4, that is, the discrete-time system $x_{k+1} = N(x_k)$ on $[0,1]^4$. Equivalently, $x_k$ is the output of a weight-tied network made of $k$ copies of $N$, or of a recurrent network with no external input, started at $x_0$. We prove that every deterministic Turing machine $M$ admits such a network $N_M$. The network can be constructed in polynomial time from $M$. Each iteration has depth $\mathrm{poly}(|M|)$. The iterates of $N_M$ simulate $M$ exactly on every encoded tape. The number of iterations is proportional to the running time of $M$. Moreover, the fourth coordinate irreversibly flags every point of the convex cube $[0,1]^4$ whose simulation reads an invalid digit. This flag is the certificate that makes hardness reductions sound on convex input regions, the regime of practical verifiers. Convex regions were previously inaccessible because of a continuity obstruction inherent to ReLU networks. The correspondence has three consequences. First, reachability for iterated width-4 ReLU networks spans the full complexity hierarchy along the single axis of the time bound: it is NP-complete for a unary bound, NEXP-complete for a binary bound and RE-complete (undecidable) with no bound. Second, two extra neurons of width suffice to extend the hardness to every common smooth activation: at width 6, the robust verification problem (a promise problem with $\delta/2\delta$ gap) is NP-complete for $\tanh$, sigmoid, GELU, Swish, ELU, and any polynomial-time-computable continuous non-polynomial activation with a polynomial-time-computable Lipschitz constant. Third, the whole spectrum transfers to discretized Neural ODEs in dimension 5.
item.dc:creator: Olivier Bournez, Johanne Cohen, Adrian Wurm

item.title: TLAPS-Bench: Formally Proving Correctness of Real-World System Specifications with TLA+ Proof System
item.description: arXiv:2611.02849v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: TLAPS-Bench is a benchmark and execution harness for constructing machine-checked proofs for real-world system specifications in TLA+ with agentic AI. Proving correctness of complex system specifications requires discovering inductive invariants, reasoning about intricate state transitions, and decomposing proofs into tractable obligations. TLAPS-Bench provides a proof harness that supports iterative proof development atop the TLA+ Proof System (TLAPS), where agents are equipped with proof tools and libraries, with safeguards against reward hacking. Using the harness, we have employed AI agents to prove desired properties for important system specifications that were not proved before, spanning cache coherence, Byzantine consensus, and write-ahead logs. TLAPS-Bench contains 265 proof targets (each encodes a property to prove) from 95 TLA+ specifications of real-world systems. We evaluated frontier AI agents, represented by Codex with GPT models, on a subset of 70 proof targets across 12 specifications. The highest-scoring model, GPT-6.1 Sol (max), proved 31 (44.3%) proof targets. The results show challenges and opportunities in end-to-end proof development.
item.dc:creator: Qian Cheng, Ruize Tang, Saad Mohammad Rafid Pial, Zhizhen Cathy Cai, Yiming Su, Jackson Clark, Munim Thahmid, Mahdiya Rahman Sukanya, Chris Newcombe, Igor Konnov, Stephan Merz, Xudong Sun, Murat Demirbas, Yu Huang, Markus Alexander Kuppe, Tianyin Xu

item.title: Generative Logic: A Deterministic Reasoning Engine
item.description: arXiv:2508.00017v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present Generative Logic (GL), a deterministic computer architecture for automated mathematical reasoning. GL starts from axiomatic definitions written in a minimalist Mathematical Programming Language (MPL) and explores a configurable region of their deductive neighborhood. The definitions are compiled into a grid of Logic Blocks (LBs). An LB applies rules by hash-table lookups, and every statement it derives keeps its complete provenance. A run generates conjectures, removes those that counterexamples refute, tries to prove the rest, reduces the proved theorems to an essential core and writes every proof as navigable HTML. An independent verifier checks every proof step. From supplied definitions, GL derives the basic laws of Peano arithmetic and Gauss's summation formula. From previously proved lemmas, further definitions and a supplied list of conjectures, it builds a proof of the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic (FTA). These proofs are also exported to Lean 4 and checked by the Lean kernel. The next step is for GL to derive the FTA as well, without supplied conjectures. GL is designed together with a hardware architecture, the Mathematical Processing Unit (MPU).
item.dc:creator: Nikolai Sergeev

item.title: Morita Rigidity for Kleene Algebras
item.description: arXiv:2510.24993v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce Morita equivalence to the study of Kleene algebras and modules. Classical characterizations of Morita-equivalent semirings such as having equivalent categories of modules and one semiring being a full idempotent corner of a finite matrix semiring over the other transfer easily to this new context. We also observe that Morita equivalence can be applied to extending and restricting scalars in Lindenbaum--Tarski algebras of propositional dynamic logics, and that an appropriately-defined category of generalized finite automata satisfies the property that when the underlying Kleene algebras are Morita equivalent then the corresponding categories of generalized automata are equivalent. But the signature results which we obtain relate to rigidity of Kleene algebras in this context. Specifically, every semiring that is Morita-equivalent to the semiring reduct of a Kleene algebra has a unique expansion to a Kleene algebra, and semiring bimodules witnessing Morita-equivalence of semirings which are reducts of Kleene algebras are already Kleene bimodules.
item.dc:creator: Luke Serafin

item.title: ScenicProver: A Framework for Compositional Probabilistic Verification of Learning-Enabled Systems
item.description: arXiv:2511.02164v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Full verification of learning-enabled cyber-physical systems (CPS) has long been intractable due to challenges including black-box components and complex real-world environments. Existing tools either provide formal guarantees for limited types of systems or test the system as a monolith, but no general framework exists for compositional analysis of learning-enabled CPS using varied verification techniques over complex real-world environments. This paper introduces a tool, ScenicProver, that aims to fill this gap by enabling the construction of sound, formally-checked assurance cases for CPS. ScenicProver is backed by a formal theory, which we lay out in this paper. ScenicProver supports: (1) environment modeling using the Scenic probabilistic programming language; (2) compositional system modeling with clear component interfaces, ranging from interpretable code to black boxes; (3) assume-guarantee contracts over those components using an extension of Linear Temporal Logic containing arbitrary Scenic expressions; (4) evidence generation through testing, formal proofs in Lean 4, and external assumptions; (5) sound combination of generated evidence using contract operators with Pacti; and (6) automatic generation of assurance cases tracking the provenance of system-level guarantees. We demonstrate its effectiveness through two case studies: one on an automatic emergency braking system with sensor fusion and one on drone safety. By leveraging manufacturer guarantees for sensors and focusing testing effort on uncertain conditions, our approach enables stronger probabilistic guarantees than monolithic testing with the same computational budget.
item.dc:creator: Eric Vin, Lucy Horowitz, Kyle A. Miller, Inigo Incer, Sanjit A. Seshia, Daniel J. Fremont

item.title: A Diagrammatic Basis for Computer Programming
item.description: arXiv:2512.07240v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Tape diagrams provide a convenient graphical notation for arrows of rig categories, i.e., categories equipped with two monoidal products, $\oplus$ and $\otimes$. In this work, we introduce Kleene-Cartesian rig categories, namely rig categories where $\otimes$ provides a Cartesian bicategory, while $\oplus$ a Kleene bicategory. We show that the associated tape diagrams can conveniently deal with imperative programs and various program logic.
item.dc:creator: Filippo Bonchi, Alessandro Di Giorgio, Elena Di Lavore

item.title: Monoidal categories graded by partial commutative monoids
item.description: arXiv:2603.16375v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Effectful categories have two classes of morphisms: pure morphisms, which form a monoidal category; and effectful morphisms, which can only be combined monoidally with central morphisms (such as the pure ones), forming a premonoidal category. This suggests seeing morphisms of an effectful category as carrying a grade that combines under the monoidal product in a partially defined manner. We axiomatize this idea with the notion of monoidal category graded by a partial commutative monoid (PCM). Monoidal categories arise as the special case of grading by the singleton PCM, and effectful categories arise from grading by a two-element PCM. Further examples include grading by powerset PCMs, modelling non-interfering parallelism for programs accessing shared resources, and grading by intervals, modelling bounded resource usage. We show that effectful categories form a coreflective subcategory of PCM-graded monoidal categories; introduce cartesian structure, recovering Freyd categories; and describe PCM-graded monoidal categories as monoids by viewing a PCM as a thin promonoidal category.
item.dc:creator: Matthew Earnshaw, Chad Nester, Mario Rom\'an

item.title: Stone Duality for Monads
item.description: arXiv:2603.25710v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce a contravariant idempotent adjunction between (i) the category of ranked monads on $\mathsf{Set}$; and (ii) the category of internal categories and internal retrofunctors in the category of locales. The left adjoint takes a monad $T$-viewed as a notion of computation, following Moggi-to its localic behaviour category $\mathsf{LB}T$. This behaviour category is understood as "the universal transition system" for interacting with $T$: its "objects" are states and the "morphisms" are transitions. On the other hand, the right adjoint takes a localic category $\mathsf{LC}$-similarly understood as a transition system-to the monad $\Gamma\mathsf{LC}$ where $(\Gamma\mathsf{LC})A$ is the set of $A$-indexed families of local sections to the source map which jointly partition the locale of objects. The fixed points of this adjunction consist of (i) hyperaffine-unary monads, i.e., those monads where term $t$ admits a read-only operation $\bar{t}$ predicting the output of $t$; and (ii) ample localic categories, i.e., whose source maps are local homeomorphisms and whose locale of objects are strongly zero-dimensional. The hyperaffine-unary monads arise in earlier works by Johnstone and Garner as a syntactic characterization of those monads with Cartesian closed Eilenberg-Moore categories. This equivalence is the Stone duality for monads; so-called because it further restricts to the classical Stone duality by viewing a Boolean algebra $B$ as a monad of $B$-partitions and the corresponding Stone space as a localic category with only identity morphisms.
item.dc:creator: Richard Garner, Alyssa Renata, Nicolas Wu

item.title: A Linear Temporal Logic of Frequencies on Series of Events
item.description: arXiv:2604.10669v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper introduces LTLFS, a linear temporal logic for reasoning about frequencies in finite series of probabilistic events. The logic conservatively extends linear temporal logic over finite traces with measure-sensitive operators that compare the empirical distribution observed at any point in a series with an independently specified target distribution. Its semantics integrates the actual sequence of events, the probability distribution governing individual outcomes, and the set of finite assignments compatible with the target frequency. This supports two complementary tasks: verifying whether an observed partial distribution is compatible with the benchmark, and predicting whether and with what probability the completed series can still satisfy it. The language can express observed and attainable frequencies, the probability of realizing a desired final distribution, and conditional probabilities for subsequent outcomes under the assumption that the benchmark is met. We establish formal properties of the operators and characterize their interaction with the temporal structure. A running example concerning representational fairness in sequential outputs from a generative AI system illustrates how the framework can distinguish temporary deviations from irrecoverable violations and support early, logically interpretable intervention. LTLFS thereby provides a symbolic foundation for runtime monitoring of evolving quantitative requirements, with applications to explainable and responsible AI.
item.dc:creator: Melissa Antonelli, Alessandro Giuseppe Buda, Leonardo Ceragioli, Ferdinando Fugazza Calda, Giuseppe Primiero

item.title: Cover Semantics for Intuitionistic Modalities
item.description: arXiv:2607.11352v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Intuitionistic modal logic (IML) has inspired several developments in programming languages including modal type systems for staging, computational effects and language-based security. IMLs are typically studied using Kripke-style relational semantics, which simplifies proofs of meta-theoretic properties, such as completeness and consistency, by making it easy to construct models. Kripke-style relational semantics, however, relies upon classical reasoning principles, which makes it unappealing from a computational perspective and unsuitable for formalization in a constructive type theory. Goldblatt provides an alternative semantics for IMLs by extending Beth-Kripke-Joyal-style "cover" semantics for intuitionistic propositional logic with relations to support modalities. Goldblatt's "relational cover" semantics overcomes classical reasoning but introduces a new limitation: it relies upon a "modal localization" condition that restricts the class of models and complicates model construction. Goldblatt bypasses this restriction by using intricate order-theoretic completion arguments to prove completeness. In this article, we present a conservative extension of relational cover semantics that alleviates this restriction and is amenable to simpler and standard model construction techniques. We formalize our semantics in Agda and prove completeness constructively in the style of Normalization by Evaluation for a variety of IMLs featuring independent box and diamond modalities.
item.dc:creator: Nachiappan Valliappan

item.title: Robustness Analysis via Horofunction Compactification
item.description: arXiv:2609.21009v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Robustness analysis plays a central role in the verification and design of computational and hybrid systems, particularly when system behaviour depends continuously on parameters subject to perturbation. Existing domain-theoretic frameworks provide a principled foundation for reasoning about such perturbations via monotone maps on lattices of closed sets. However, these frameworks face significant limitations when the underlying state space is not locally compact, as is the case for the infinite-dimensional spaces that arise in analysis, machine learning, and control theory (e.g., $\ell_p$ and $L_p$ spaces). In these settings, the lattice of closed subsets fails to be continuous, and classical compactifications either sacrifice precision or lack computable structure. We propose Gromov's horofunction compactification as a new tool for robustness analysis over a class of separable metric spaces of practical importance, including separable reflexive Banach spaces. Given a metric space $\mathbb{S}$, we show that its horofunction extension yields a compact metric space together with a Lipschitz embedding, which enables robust approximations of monotone maps via Scott-continuous maps on the compactified domain. For separable spaces, the horofunction compactification is metrizable, which provides a path toward effective domain-theoretic constructions.
item.dc:creator: Harrison Bennett, Amin Farjudian

item.title: An Exponential Succinctness Gap between Three-Variable Logic and the Calculus of Relations
item.description: arXiv:2609.26778v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Three-variable first-order logic ($\mathrm{FO}^3$) and the calculus of relations (CoR) define the same binary queries, an equivalence that goes back to Tarski's work in the 1940s. The classical translation from $\mathrm{FO}^3$ to CoR is single-exponential, but it has remained open whether this blowup is necessary. We prove that it is, even over finite structures and even for circuits that share subterms. Our proof introduces a new technique: we modify a single finite structure in exponentially many local ways, each changing the answer of a short $\mathrm{FO}^3$ formula $\varphi$. In any CoR circuit $C$ equivalent to $\varphi$, only compositions of binary relations can notice these modifications, and each composition can notice at most two; thus, $C$ requires exponentially many compositions. The same technique gives an exponential succinctness gap between $\mathrm{FO}^3$ and $\mathrm{FO}^2$, and exponential lower bounds for matrix query languages over the Boolean and tropical semirings, where the analogous question was also open.
item.dc:creator: Yuya Uezato, Yoshiki Nakamura

item.title: Proofs Without Nominals: G\"odel's Ontological Argument, its Shallow Embedding, and the Open Questions of the Monatshefte Notes
item.description: arXiv:2609.36279v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The shallow embedding of higher-order modal logic in classical higher-order logic, used in Benzm\"uller and Scott's Notes on G\"odel's and Scott's variants of the ontological argument, reaches beyond the modal object language: its quantifiers range over domains containing the nominals and satisfaction operators of hybrid logic. A proof using one proves a theorem of the embedding, not necessarily of the modal logic. Whether a result is one of the modal logic can be settled by replaying it in an explicit calculus, or, more cheaply and for all results at once, by analysing what the embedding's proofs substitute. Every statement the Notes prove has a proof in the embedding substituting nothing outside the object language, 294 of them explicit. The Notes' own proofs substitute none either; what it flags are terms a prover introduced. A soundness theorem over general models closed under the object language, and a sentence of that language the embedding proves but which fails in such a model, fix what the certificate says. The Notes' three open questions are settled too, without nominals, but by the empty instance of the conjunction axiom, too cheaply to convince. Generalised to G\"odel's "any number of summands", the axiom covers the empty conjunction and the singleton. This article restricts it to at least two different conjuncts, a non-degenerate reading of G\"odel's footnote, and settles them again without nominals. In effect only the empty conjunction is excluded; the singleton comes back with the other axioms. In one variant the restriction refutes the possible existence of a God-like being; the answers return, with no side condition, once the Notes' non-emptiness clause is confined to G\"odel's essence. Every theorem here is verified in Isabelle/HOL and independently in Lean 4, the separating model in its propositional part; the countermodels are Nitpick's, checked by the build.
item.dc:creator: Christoph Benzm\"uller

item.title: Concurrent Strategies as Street Fibrations
item.description: arXiv:2609.37815v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Concurrent games and strategies based on event structures are an established and expressive model of interactive computation. In this paper we revisit the problem of equipping this model with symmetry. Symmetry is essential for many applications, but it is also a source of mathematical complexity, not least because strategies with symmetry can be compared up to several distinct notions of equivalence. Our first contribution is a complete characterization of two classes of strategies for which composition admits an identity. For these two classes the identity laws hold, respectively, up to a "weak" and a "strong" notion of equivalence. The main result is that the weak class of strategies corresponds precisely to those inducing Street fibrations over the game. We also show how the established "thin" approach to symmetry also fits in this general framework. A second contribution is a formal connection between games and setoid-valued profunctors. This follows a long tradition of relating games and relational models, but here additionally includes a very general model of symmetries. Our characterization of strategies as Street fibrations makes the connection to profunctors significantly easier to establish.
item.dc:creator: Hugo Paquet, Glynn Winskel

item.title: An explicit shuffle construction of the homotopy span model of differential linear logic
item.description: arXiv:2610.10789v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We give a direct and explicit construction of the homotopy span model of linear logic originally formulated by Melli\`es using abstract homotopy theory in the Quillen category Cat of small categories equipped with its natural model structure. Following the principles of homotopy theory, the formulas and proofs of linear logic are interpreted in the model as small categories up to categorical equivalence, the notion of weak homotopy equivalence underlying the natural Quillen model structure on Cat. Here, we explain how the original interpretation of proofs as fibrant spans can be replaced by a more liberal interpretation of proofs as separately fibrant spans. This relaxation from fibrant spans to separately fibrant spans enables us to give a simple and intuitive description of the homotopy span model, where the axiom and cut links are interpreted as identity spans, and where the symmetries of the exponential modality are captured by a shuffle structure on the interpretation of proofs.
item.dc:creator: Paul-Andr\'e Melli\`es, Federico Olimpieri, Lionel Vaux Auclair

item.title: Compact Quantitative Equational Theories as Monad Restrictions
item.description: arXiv:2610.13201v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Proofs in quantitative algebra are, generally, infinite objects due to the presence of infinitary rules in the deductive apparatus. A quantitative equational theory is called compact if all its consequences are derivable by means of finite proofs, that is, proofs not using any instances of the infinitary rules. This definition is purely logical. In this work we give an equivalent, but categorical, characterisation based on the notion of monad restriction.
item.dc:creator: Matteo Mio, Colin Riba

item.title: Unit: a type checker for dependent type theory
item.description: arXiv:2610.34264v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present Unit, a type checker for dependent type theory with a module system in the tradition of Automath and a uniform treatment of definitions. There is no unification, no instance search, no tactics and no unfolding heuristic, so the work of checking can be observed and compared with the informal proof. With Unit we have checked a model of univalent type theory, synthetic algebraic geometry, and synthetic Stone duality with its cohomology, and results in commutative algebra, like finite free resolutions and Zariski Main Theorem. These developments show that a small, uniform system supports substantial mathematics, and give concrete reasons to reconsider the complexity routinely accepted in proof assistants.
item.dc:creator: Thierry Coquand

item.title: A Quantitative Interpretation of Useful Call-by-Value
item.description: arXiv:2610.40154v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this work, we present the first semantic interpretation of useful call-by-value evaluation through a non-idempotent intersection type system called U. One first contribution of this paper is a characterisation of termination of useful call-by-value evaluation via U-typability. That is, a term is typable in system U if and only if it terminates in the useful call-by-value strategy. As a second contribution, we show that system U provides a quantitative interpretation for useful call-by-value evaluation, offering exact step-count information for program evaluation. Even though the specification of the operational semantics of useful evaluation is highly complex, system U is notably simple. As far as we know, system U is one of the scarce quantitative type systems capturing exactly the substitution step-count for variables and abstractions in an open call-by-value strategy. Our third contribution is a termination-equivalence result between standard call-by-value, which may perform erasing reductions, and useful call-by-value, which is non-erasing. To establish this result, we introduce a non-erasing restriction of standard call-by-value, a refinement that serves as an intermediate calculus bridging standard and useful call-by-value. We show that all three calculi have the same termination behaviour, and hence induce the same observational equivalence.
item.dc:creator: Pablo Barenbaum, Delia Kesner, Mariana Milicich

item.title: More on Higher Order Busy Beaver Functions
item.description: arXiv:2507.20321v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In this paper, we extend the Busy Beaver function to a class of higher order Busy Beaver functions based on Turing oracle machine. We prove some results about the relation between decidability of number theoretical formula and higher order Busy Beaver functions, and the relations between computability of max-min partial recursive functions, limit partial recursive functions and higher order Busy Beaver functions. We also present some conjectures on higher order Busy Beaver functions.
item.dc:creator: Zining Cao

item.title: Domain size asymptotics for Markov logic networks
item.description: arXiv:2509.04192v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A Markov logic network (MLN) $\mathbb{M}$ determines a probability distribution $\mathbb{P}_n^\mathbb{M}$ on the set $\mathbf{W}_n$ of structures, or ``possible worlds'', with domain $\{1, \ldots, n\}$. We study the properties of such distributions as $n$ tends to infinity. We show that with mild assumptions on an MLN $\mathbb{M}$ with one soft constraint with an arbitrary positive weight the distribution $\mathbb{P}_n^\mathbb{M}$ will behave quite differently from the uniform distribution $\mathbb{P}_n^{uni}$ on $\mathbf{W}_n$ for all sufficiently large $n$. For a language with only one relation symbol $R$ which has arity 1 we give an almost complete characterization of the possible asymptotic behaviours of $\mathbb{P}_n^\mathbb{M}$ as $n \to \infty$, where $\mathbb{M}$ may be any MLN for this language. The asymptotic behaviour depends on the soft constraints and weights of the MLN. This characterization is used to show that if the language under consideration contains at least one relation symbol of arity 1 then the following holds: (a) There is an MLN $\mathbb{M}$ such that for every lifted Bayesian network (LBN) $\mathbb{G}$ there are infinitely many $n$ such that $\mathbb{M}$ and $\mathbb{G}$ determine different distributions on $\mathbf{W}_n$. (b) There is an LBN $\mathbb{G}$ such that for every MLN $\mathbb{M}$ there are infinitely many $n$ such that $\mathbb{G}$ and $\mathbb{M}$ determine different distributions on $\mathbf{W}_n$. We also show that, in the limit, the weight dimension and the domain size dimension may behave completely differently.
item.dc:creator: Vera Koponen

item.title: Monadic Second-Order Logic of Permutations
item.description: arXiv:2511.02386v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Permutations can be viewed as pairs of linear orders, or more formally as models over a signature consisting of two binary relation symbols. This approach was adopted by Albert, Bouvel and F\'eray, who studied the expressibility of first-order logic in this setting. We focus our attention on monadic second-order logic. Our results go in two directions. First, we investigate the expressive power of monadic second-order logic. We exhibit natural properties of permutations that can be expressed in monadic second-order logic but not in first-order logic. Additionally, we show that the property of having a fixed point is inexpressible even in monadic second-order logic. Secondly, we focus on the complexity of monadic second-order model checking. We show that there is an algorithm deciding if a permutation $\pi$ satisfies a given monadic second-order sentence $\varphi$ in time $f(|\varphi|, \operatorname{tw}(\pi)) \cdot n$ for some computable function $f$ where $n = |\pi|$ and $\operatorname{tw}(\pi)$ is the tree-width of $\pi$. On the other hand, we prove that the problem remains hard even when we restrict the permutation $\pi$ to a fixed hereditary class $\mathcal{C}$ with mild assumptions on $\mathcal{C}$.
item.dc:creator: V\'it Jel\'inek, Michal Opler

item.title: Formal Evidence Generation for Assurance Cases for Robotic Software Models
item.description: arXiv:2602.03550v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Robotics and Autonomous Systems are increasingly deployed in safety-critical domains, so that demonstrating their safety is essential. Assurance Cases (ACs) provide structured arguments supported by evidence, but generating and maintaining this evidence is labour-intensive, error-prone, and difficult to keep consistent as systems evolve. We present a model-based approach to systematically generating AC evidence by embedding formal verification into the assurance workflow. The approach addresses three challenges: systematically deriving formal assertions from natural language requirements using templates, orchestrating multiple formal verification tools to handle diverse property types, and integrating formal evidence production into the workflow. Leveraging RoboChart, a domain-specific modelling language with formal semantics, we combine model checking and theorem proving in our approach. Structured requirements are automatically transformed into formal assertions using predefined templates, and verification results are automatically integrated as evidence. Case studies demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.
item.dc:creator: Fang Yan, Simon Foster, Ana Cavalcanti, Ibrahim Habli, James Baxter

item.title: A Simple Categorical Calculus of Interacting Processes
item.description: arXiv:2603.18321v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present a calculus that models a simple sort of process interaction. Our calculus consists of a collection of terms together with a rewrite relation, parameterised by an arbitrary multicategory whose morphisms we understand as non-interactive processes. We show that our calculus is confluent and terminating, and that terms modulo the induced convertibility relation form a virtual double category. We relate our calculus to the free cornering of a monoidal category, which is a double-categorical model of process interaction that is similar in spirit to the calculus presented herein. Precisely, we construct a functor from the virtual double category given by our calculus into the underlying virtual double category of the free cornering of the free monoidal category on the multicategory of non-interacting processes. If we think of the terms of our calculus as programs and the rewriting system as an operational semantics for these programs, this functor gives a sound denotational semantics for our calculus in terms of the free cornering.
item.dc:creator: Chad Nester, Niels Voorneveld

item.title: Isomorphism Is Not Enough: An Agentic Audit of Verified Code Generation in Lean
item.description: arXiv:2605.23772v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Agentic systems have recently emerged as state-of-the-art approaches for automated theorem proving in formal mathematics. To assess how far these capabilities extend to program verification and how reliably existing benchmarks can measure them, we audit CLEVER, a Lean 4 benchmark for verifiable code generation, using three independent agentic stacks based on Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5.4, and Kimi K2.5. Our audit finds arguably erroneous reference specifications in 80 of 161 entries, each accepted by the benchmark's authors, distills a taxonomy of benchmark errors, and exposes structural limitations of isomorphism-based scoring, whose signal breaks down when generated and reference specifications formalize different yet defensible readings. In the process, the stacks generate arguably valid specifications for up to 98.8% of entries, certify implementations against sound reference specifications for up to 92.3%, and reach up to 96.2% end-to-end success over entries with sound premises, suggesting that CLEVER no longer stresses modern agentic provers as much as its design intended. Looking ahead, we translate our findings into recommendations for future work, with our error analysis doubling as a repair list for CLEVER and a heuristic checklist for the next generation of benchmarks.
item.dc:creator: Alessandro Sosso, Akhil Arora, Bas Spitters

item.title: The category of nominal sets is locally monoidal closed
item.description: arXiv:2609.22551v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The category Nom of nominal sets was proposed by Pitts and Gabbay as a setting for the semantics of abstract syntax with variable bindings. It is well-known that Nom is a topos, also known as the Schanuel topos, and in particular it follows that Nom is locally closed, i.e., every slice category Nom/X is cartesian-closed. In this paper, we show that Nom has a much stronger property: every monoidal (closed) structure on Nom induces a monoidal (closed) structure on all slice categories Nom/X. One monoidal closed structure of particular interest on Nom is the separated product A * B, whose right adjoint A -* B is called the separated function space. In particular, it follows that Nom is locally separatedly closed.
item.dc:creator: Fahimeh Bayeh, Peng Fu, Peter Selinger

item.title: A Witnessing Duality for ReLU Network Depth
item.description: arXiv:2610.38281v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A depth lower bound for ReLU networks asserts that every sufficiently shallow network fails on some input. What does a proof of such a bound compute? We study this question for exact computation of the maximum of $n$ real inputs, with depth measured by the number of hidden layers. For every separately fixed prime $q$ and depth bound $K$, we give a uniform $\mathsf{TC}^0$ refuter for rational networks with at most $K$ hidden layers and more than $q^K$ inputs, provided that the reduced denominators of their nonbias weights are not divisible by $q$. Biases may be arbitrary rationals. The refuter finds a rational input on which the network fails, and its correctness is provable in $\mathbf{VTC}^0$, the bounded-arithmetic theory of uniform constant-depth threshold computation. The underlying numerical depth lower bound follows from Averkov, Hojny and Merkert (ICLR 2025), extending Haase, Hertrich and Loho (ICLR 2023); our contribution is an internal proof that makes its geometric argument into a feasible refuter. On the construction side, $\mathbf{VTC}^0$ verifies locally checkable certificates for the balanced integer-weight maximum network of depth $\lceil\log_2 n\rceil$. At $q=2$, the construction and refuter meet: for each fixed $K$, the theory verifies that integer-nonbias-weight networks with arbitrary rational biases can compute the maximum with at most $K$ hidden layers exactly when $n\le 2^K$. We also give certified rational constructions of polynomial encoding length and depth $O(\log n/\log\log n)$. These results instantiate a witnessing duality: bounded proofs of certified existence and of refutation correspond, respectively, to threshold-computable constructors and refuters whose guarantees the theory proves.
item.dc:creator: Dimitrios Myrisiotis

item.title: One Polynomial Field for Every Euler Step and the Flow: Polynomial Dynamics for P and PSPACE
item.description: arXiv:2610.40025v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We construct, for each deterministic Turing machine that halts on all inputs, one polynomial vector field with rational coefficients that performs the same logical computation at unit Euler step, at every smaller or variable step in $(0,1]$ with divergent sum, and along the flow. This unifies discrete-time and continuous-time computation by polynomial dynamics, which earlier characterizations treated separately. For a machine making $T$ transitions in space $H$, a logical scale $h=2^{-s}$ with $s=O(H)$ suffices, with physical time $O(s(T+s))$, drift disturbances up to $h^{2K}$ for a fixed exponent $K$, and $2Ks+3$ fractional bits at unit step. On a fixed compact domain, polynomial time and robust eventual decision characterize P and PSPACE, respectively, with polynomial scale thresholds and no supplied stabilization horizon in the space case. Without sign, floor or conditional primitives, margin amplification at bounded speed, overlapping polynomial gates and interval-product estimates give the common realization, from which we derive shared logical traces, fixed-field PSPACE-complete prediction and a robust safety family with polynomial certificates common to all Euler steps and the flow.
item.dc:creator: Olivier Bournez
